We gather in this forum to discuss the decline and preservation of the Occident [in German, Abendland, evening-land] against treason from within and dissolution from without. However in my amateur anthropological reading, I asked myself another question that did not immediately present itself with an answer. What precisely is Western civilisation; what is it that distinguishes us from all other nations? Which nations can rightfully consider themselves to be Western? Most of the possible definitions of the West that immediately came to my thoughts, and I find would likely come to yours, have failed for multiple reasons:

  • The inheritors of ancient Greece and then Rome. This answer was the first to come to mind, yet it seems too general. The most prominent counter-example would be that of the Saracens; though they did very little to advance the superior culture whose land they occupied, and indeed eventually destroyed it, the culture they did adopt was taken from it. (Confer AndrÃ© Servier's Islam and the Psychology of the Musulman; in large part the Arabian culture was merely the Bedouin's failed attempts to comprehend Roman civilisation.)
  • Members of the white race. Though there is indeed a distinct Caucasoid race (internal subdivisions per Ripley, 1899, notwithstanding and here inconsequential regardless), its range extends southwards into Arabia and Barbary and as far south as Abyssinia, yet it would be foolish to include them as part of the West because of mere physical similarity. The difference between the Spaniard and Libyan, or Greek and Turk, is more of cultural (and especially religious, but more later) than racial nature. Moreover this definition would include the Aryans proper, that is to say Persia and India, though they are both distinctly Oriental and always have been.
  • The West as Christendom. Until some time within the last two centuries, this notion may have been sufficient (albeit with the exception of Abyssinia). Literature had traditionally defined the West with the Roman church and eventually the Protestant churches, excluding the GrÃ¦co-Russian Orthodox Church. This translated well enough into the Cold War, yet with the events of the last quarter-century I am hesitant to define Russia and Servia still as Oriental; also the Byzantines, at least until the Mahometan conquests, maintained distinct connexions with the West. (Cf. Mohammed and Charlemagne, that also distinguishes Roman from Western civilisation.) Moreover the light of Christ has spread into trans-Saharan Africa in the last century, though this has not made its inhabitants any more Western. The status of America south of the Rio Grande is also ambivalent, as is the status of heathen Greece and Rome, and perhaps England and Scandinavia. I as a Christian support the spread of the Gospel as a matter of course, yet accepting Christ alone does not define the West.
  • Monogamy. The rÃ´le of monogamy, a correlation that I had already observed elsewhere is certainly important and helps to bridge the gap between us and our heathen forebearers, and even bears some modern relevance; I understand that many nominal Christians in Africa continue to take many wives. However I feel that merely correcting these heresies does not make the Cushite Western.
  • Industrial civilisation. This definition is obviously limited to the last two centuries, though it does neatly correlate with the movements of Asiatic countries to Westernise, including the most successful example of Japan and more recently Corea, and the failed attempts of Egypt, Turkey and Persia. Still it ignores the underlying cultural differences that a modern economy itself does not rectify.

As is clear, I have yet to form a definitive answer and I hence present the question to you. We stand by Europa our mother, and we stand by Western civilisation, yet what precisely is it? I open the question for you to discuss.
